title: Bush Medicine: Tea Tree Oil and Indigenous Knowledge
subtitle: How an Aboriginal medicine treats infection, and who should benefit from it
subject: Biology
syllabusDotPoints: investigate the contemporary application of Aboriginal protocols in the development of particular medicines and biological materials in Australia and how recognition and protection of Indigenous cultural and intellectual property is important, for example: bush medicine, smoke bush in Western Australia
Describe the use of an Aboriginal bush medicine in treating disease (tea tree oil, Kakadu plum or emu bush)
inquiryQuestion: How can the spread of infectious diseases be controlled?
lessonIntent: Students can describe how the Bundjalung people used tea tree to treat infection and how tea tree oil acts on microbes, and explain why consent and benefit sharing protect Indigenous cultural and intellectual property.
examSkill: Describe the use of a named Aboriginal bush medicine in treating disease, including its active compound and mechanism, and distinguish ethical bioprospecting from biopiracy.

introVoiceover.text: Welcome back to HSC Biology. Today, bush medicine, tea tree oil and Indigenous knowledge. Let's get into it.

scenes.caption: Bush Medicine: Tea Tree Oil and Indigenous Knowledge

scenes.heading: From crushed leaves to a global industry
scenes.body: The Bundjalung people used tea tree leaves on wounds and for coughs and colds. Today tea tree oil is sold around the world.
scenes.callout: When Aboriginal knowledge becomes a product, who should benefit?
scenes.caption: Bundjalung knowledge of tea tree became a worldwide antiseptic industry.

voiceover.text: OK, picture the wetlands of north eastern New South Wales, Bundjalung Country. For a very long time, Bundjalung people have used the leaves of a local tree, Melaleuca alternifolia, to treat illness. Crushed leaves were inhaled for coughs and colds, applied to wounds, and soaked to make a wash for sore throats. In the nineteen twenties, a government chemist tested the oil from those leaves and reported strong antiseptic activity, and a commercial industry grew from it. Today tea tree oil is sold around the world. So two questions drive this lesson. How does tea tree oil actually treat infection? And when Aboriginal knowledge becomes a product, who should benefit?

scenes.heading: Bush medicine is living knowledge
scenes.body: Bush medicine is the use of native plants, animals and minerals for healing by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, built up over tens of thousands of years.

bullets.text: Knowledge belongs to particular communities and Country, and some of it is not shared publicly.
It is empirical: repeated use, careful observation of outcomes, and refinement over generations.
Examples include tea tree oil, Kakadu plum and emu bush, each still used today.

scenes.secondary: Kakadu plum is exceptionally rich in vitamin C, and emu bush (Eremophila) is being studied for antibacterial compounds.
scenes.callout: Tens of thousands of years of careful observation, held by communities.
scenes.caption: Bush medicine is empirical, community-held knowledge of native plants, animals and minerals.

voiceover.text: Let's start with what bush medicine is. It's the use of native plants, animals and minerals for healing by Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, built up over tens of thousands of years and still practised today. Two things matter here. First, it isn't one single body of knowledge. It belongs to particular communities and their Country, and some of it is culturally restricted and not shared publicly, so it should be discussed with respect. Second, it's empirical knowledge, in the truest sense, built from repeated use, careful observation of what works, and refinement over generations. Kakadu plum is exceptionally rich in vitamin C, and emu bush is being studied for antibacterial compounds. But today we'll focus on one medicine in depth, tea tree oil.

scenes.heading: How tea tree oil treats infection
scenes.body: Tea tree oil is distilled from Melaleuca alternifolia leaves. Its main active compound is terpinen-4-ol.

bullets.text: Traditional use: crushed leaves for wounds, skin infections, coughs, colds and sore throats.
Terpinen-4-ol damages microbial cell membranes, so ions and cell contents leak out.
Active against many bacteria, including MRSA, and fungi such as tinea and Candida.
Trials support it for acne and tinea; it is used on the skin and is toxic if swallowed.

scenes.secondary: Because it attacks membranes rather than one enzyme, it acts on bacteria and fungi alike, but it is a topical treatment, not a replacement for antibiotics in serious infections.
scenes.callout: Break the membrane, and the microbe dies.
scenes.caption: Terpinen-4-ol disrupts microbial membranes; tea tree oil treats skin infections topically.

voiceover.text: So how does it work? Tea tree oil is distilled from the leaves, and its main active compound is terpinen four ol. These oily compounds dissolve into the lipid membranes of microbes, making them leaky, so ions and other cell contents spill out, and the cell's respiration is disrupted until it dies. Because it attacks the membrane, rather than one specific enzyme, it works against a broad range of microbes, many bacteria, including the resistant Staphylococcus called MRSA, and fungi like the ones behind tinea and thrush. That fits the traditional uses on wounds and skin. Modern trials back some of this up. A five percent tea tree gel reduced acne about as well as a standard treatment, working more slowly but with fewer side effects, and stronger solutions improved tinea of the feet. One vital safety point, it's used on the skin, and it's toxic if swallowed.

scenes.heading: The words you need

bullets.text: Bioprospecting: searching biological resources for useful compounds, ideally with consent and benefit sharing.
Biopiracy: commercial use of biological resources or traditional knowledge without consent or benefit sharing.
Free prior informed consent: permission from a community before research or commercial use of their knowledge.
Benefit sharing: a fair return of financial, scientific or social benefits to the knowledge-holding community.

scenes.callout: Bioprospecting and biopiracy can be the same act; only the process differs.
scenes.caption: Bioprospecting, biopiracy, free prior informed consent, benefit sharing.

voiceover.text: Now the words behind the ethics. Bioprospecting is searching biological resources for useful compounds, and done properly, that means with consent and benefit sharing. Biopiracy is the commercial use of biological resources or traditional knowledge without consent and without benefit sharing. Here's the crucial insight, the two can involve the exact same plant and the exact same knowledge, and the difference is entirely the process. That process has two parts. Free prior informed consent means genuine permission from a community before any research or commercial use begins. And benefit sharing means a fair return of financial, scientific or social benefits to the community that held the knowledge.

scenes.heading: Bioprospecting versus biopiracy
scenes.body: The same discovery can be ethical or exploitative depending entirely on whether the community consented and shared in the benefits.

bullets.text: Ethical bioprospecting: consent obtained first, a benefit-sharing agreement in place, work on agreed terms.
Biopiracy: the community is never consulted and receives nothing from the commercial product.
Patent examiners search written records, so oral knowledge can be missed and wrongly patented.

scenes.secondary: The Nagoya Protocol, in force from 2014 and ratified by Australia in 2022, requires prior informed consent, mutually agreed terms and benefit sharing, but it is not retrospective.
scenes.callout: Same plant, same knowledge, opposite ethics.
scenes.caption: Bioprospecting versus biopiracy turns on consent and benefit sharing; the Nagoya Protocol addresses it.

voiceover.text: So let's make the distinction concrete. Ethical bioprospecting means engaging the community before any research starts, obtaining free prior informed consent, agreeing how benefits will be shared, and only then proceeding. Biopiracy is the opposite, where the community is never consulted and receives nothing. And there's a legal gap that lets it happen. Patents should only be granted for genuinely new inventions, but examiners search written records for what's called prior art, and knowledge passed down orally won't show up there. The international response is the Nagoya Protocol, in force from twenty fourteen and ratified by Australia in twenty twenty two, which requires prior informed consent, mutually agreed terms and benefit sharing. But it isn't retrospective, so it can't fix older cases. When the tea tree industry began in the nineteen twenties, for example, there were no consent or benefit sharing requirements at all.

scenes.heading: Analyse the smoke bush case
scenes.question: Researchers collected smoke bush in Western Australia under a standard plant-collection permit. Anti-HIV compounds from it were later patented and licensed without consulting local Aboriginal communities. Explain why this is biopiracy and why the communities had no legal recourse at the time.
scenes.coachNote: Apply the consent and benefit-sharing test, then explain the prior-art gap.
steps: The community's traditional knowledge was used commercially without consent or benefit sharing.
That is the definition of biopiracy: the same knowledge, used without a fair process.
A collection permit did not require community consultation, so the agency acted within the rules of the time.
The oral knowledge was not in any written patent database, so it could not block the patent as prior art.
Answer: biopiracy by the consent test; no recourse because permits ignored community consent and oral knowledge was invisible to patent law ✓
scenes.caption: Smoke bush: biopiracy by the consent test, with no recourse under old patent law.

voiceover.text: Let's analyse the case the syllabus names, smoke bush in Western Australia. Researchers collected smoke bush under a standard plant collection permit, and anti HIV compounds from it were later patented and licensed, without consulting the local Aboriginal communities who knew the plant. Explain why this is biopiracy, and why those communities had no legal recourse at the time. Step one, apply the test. Was there consent? No. Was there benefit sharing? No. So by definition it's biopiracy. Step two, why no recourse? The permit system didn't require consent from Aboriginal communities, so the collectors were acting within the rules as they stood. Step three, the prior art gap. The knowledge was held orally, so it wasn't in any written patent record, and it couldn't block the patent. That's why protocols requiring consent and benefit sharing matter so much.

scenes.heading: Two traps
scenes.body: Trap 1: thinking bush medicine only counts once Western science confirms it. It has value within its own knowledge system; validation adds a different kind of evidence.
scenes.secondary: Trap 2: thinking natural means safe or cures everything. Tea tree oil is toxic if swallowed, can irritate skin, and is not a substitute for antibiotics in serious infections.
scenes.mistakeTag: Validation, and natural does not mean safe
scenes.callout: Validation is not legitimacy; natural is not automatically safe.
scenes.caption: Bush medicine stands on its own; tea tree oil is effective but not harmless.

voiceover.text: Two traps to avoid. Trap one, thinking bush medicine only becomes legitimate once Western science has confirmed it. That's a hierarchical view of knowledge, and it's not accurate either. This knowledge represents thousands of years of careful observation in its own right. Lab studies and trials add a different kind of evidence, which is useful for things like regulatory approval, but they don't make the knowledge more valid, and they don't transfer ownership of it. Trap two, thinking that natural means safe, or that a bush medicine cures everything. Tea tree oil is effective on the skin, but it's toxic if swallowed, it can irritate skin, and it's not a substitute for antibiotics in a serious infection. Describe what it does, where, and how.

scenes.heading: Quick check
scenes.question: A student claims tea tree oil works 'just like penicillin'. Using the way each acts on microbes, evaluate this claim.
answerSteps: Penicillin blocks the building of bacterial cell walls, so it only works on bacteria.
Tea tree oil's terpinen-4-ol damages cell membranes, so it acts on bacteria and fungi.
Penicillin can be taken internally to treat systemic infections; tea tree oil is used on the skin and is toxic if swallowed.
Both are antimicrobial, so the claim is partly right about the outcome but wrong about the mechanism and use.
Answer: the claim is inaccurate; the targets, range of microbes and route of use all differ ✓
scenes.caption: Penicillin targets bacterial cell walls and is systemic; tea tree oil disrupts membranes and is topical.

voiceover.text: Quick check. A student claims tea tree oil works just like penicillin. Using the way each acts on microbes, evaluate that claim. Pause and reason it through. Right. Penicillin blocks bacteria from building their cell walls, so it only works on bacteria. Tea tree oil's terpinen four ol damages cell membranes, so it acts on bacteria and fungi. Penicillin can be taken internally to treat infections throughout the body, while tea tree oil is used on the skin and is toxic if swallowed. So the student is partly right, because both kill microbes, but wrong about the mechanism, the range of microbes and the way each is used. Overall, the claim is inaccurate.

scenes.heading: Lock it in
points: Bush medicine is empirical, community-held knowledge refined over tens of thousands of years.
The Bundjalung people used crushed tea tree leaves for wounds, coughs, colds and sore throats.
Tea tree oil's terpinen-4-ol damages microbial membranes; it treats skin infections topically and is toxic if swallowed.
Bioprospecting and biopiracy can use the same knowledge; consent and benefit sharing make the difference.
Oral knowledge can slip past patent law, as in the smoke bush case; the Nagoya Protocol helps but is not retrospective.

scenes.caption: Five takeaways: bush medicine, Bundjalung tea tree use, how it works, consent and benefit sharing, smoke bush.

voiceover.text: Let's lock it in. First, bush medicine is empirical, community held knowledge refined over tens of thousands of years. Second, Bundjalung people used crushed tea tree leaves to treat wounds, coughs, colds and sore throats. Third, tea tree oil's terpinen four ol damages microbial membranes, so it treats skin infections caused by bacteria and fungi, but it's toxic if swallowed. Fourth, bioprospecting and biopiracy can use the same knowledge, and what makes the difference is consent and benefit sharing. And fifth, oral knowledge can slip past patent law, as in the smoke bush case, and the Nagoya Protocol helps, but it isn't retrospective. Whenever you describe a bush medicine, name the plant, how communities used it, its active compound and how it acts on the pathogen. See you next lesson.
